title: User Profiling and Personalization through Activity Monitoring
description: This discussion explores the methods for creating user profiles, including analyzing web activity and social media content like tweets. It then focuses on leveraging these profiles to customize information retrieval, search results, and personalized recommendations.
summary: The transcript discusses two main areas: the generation of user profiles and the application of those profiles for personalization. Regarding user profiles, it questions the viability of creating profiles by monitoring general web activities and analyzing data from platforms like tweets and Twitter content. Furthermore, it examines the practical application of these profiles in information retrieval, specifically asking if profiles can be used to customize search results and provide better results to users. Finally, the discussion highlights the potential to customize recommendations and suggestions during the search process, noting that the team has achieved these results.

title: Semantic Profiling and Knowledge Management through User Interaction Networks
description: This talk discusses using semantic profiles derived from textual content to exploit buried organizational knowledge and generate user expertise networks. The research focuses on creating dynamic profiles to identify experts and understand collaboration patterns within knowledge-based groups.
summary: This presentation details research aimed at exploiting knowledge buried within organizations by generating semantic profiles of users based on their information communication exchanges. The researchers found that using semantic concepts is a highly effective measure for identifying similar users and mapping expertise. A tool was developed to visualize these clusters, showing how users interact across various research fields, highlighting that collaboration often occurs between different research groups rather than within tightly defined groups. The system allows users to search for topics and suggest relevant experts, and clicking on a user reveals related communication history. The team concluded that semantic profiling is superior to traditional keyword/entity profiling for knowledge management. The discussion also addressed challenges related to organizational knowledge management, such as the definition of experts, the use of dynamic profiles to prioritize emails, and significant concerns regarding privacy, security, and access control when implementing these systems in a real-world organizational context.

title: Leveraging Email Data for Organizational Knowledge Management and User Profiling
description: This talk outlines a threefold approach to analyzing informal organizational communication (emails), focusing on extracting features, building user profiles, and visualizing organizational networks and expertise.
summary: The presentation details a methodology for processing informal organizational communication, specifically emails, to build user profiles and facilitate knowledge management. The process begins by collecting features from emails, such as keywords, named entities, and concepts, using tools like Java Automatic Term Recognition and WikiFight. These features are then used to generate user profiles, which are subsequently leveraged for organizational insights. Data collection involves capturing detailed email metadata (e.g., meeting details) and archiving emails for later processing. Visualization methods are crucial, utilizing tools like Simnet to create a radiograph of users and color-code communication, and employing similarity measures to plot relationships between users. The presentation explores different layout approaches, including force-directed and radial layouts, to effectively visualize interpersonal relationships and identify organizational expertise.

title: Measuring User Similarity through Semantic Profiles
description: This research explores how effectively semantic features in user profiles can be used to infer similarity among individuals, comparing the results against human judgment. The study measures similarity using various behavioral and social features and validates these findings by gathering participants' perceived similarity ratings.
summary: The research addresses the challenge of measuring user similarity by profiling individuals based on binary functions and various shared features (e.g., geography, age, interests, social interactions, and Facebook data). The primary goal is to determine whether increasing the level of semantics in user profiles improves the accuracy of inferred similarity compared to current methods. To measure this, the researchers used the Jaccard index to quantify similarity across all collected data types. Finally, human judgment was incorporated by asking participants to rate their perceived similarity with colleagues based on professional and social points of interest using a 1-to-10 scale.
